newsitem.title: USA: Spin magazine founder to launch new publication.
newsitem.headline: Spin magazine founder to launch new publication.

text.p: A new pop culture magazine aimed at young males is set to compete with the likes of Rolling Stone and Details when it hits newsstands next year, its publisher said Thursday.

Bob Guccione Jr., who co-founded Spin magazine in 1985 and sold it last month, told Reuters he is now working on a magazine called Gear, which he envisages will be the first step in a diversified publishing empire. The first two issues of Gear, beginning September 1998, will be quarterly, and then it will become a monthly. Initial circulation will be 200,000.

The namesake son of the founder of Penthouse magazine is working with Boston-based investment bank Fechtor, Detwiler to raise about $10 million in start-up capital, although he will chip in for a majority stake. Spin was sold to the owners if Vibe magazine for $42 million, and Guccione's share was $16.5 million. Additionally, the bank will help him scout for acquisitions.

Gear will be targeted at 18- to 30-year-old males, and will cover pop culture, fashion and investigative reporting. But what he described as "this current trend to presume that all men are interested in flattening their stomachs" is one he will gladly leave to his competitors.

"Young men are very romantic, very idealistic and very escapist," said Guccione, who is 41. "They really want a magazine they can read that is hip, exciting, very of-the- moment, has a great sense of humor, is substantial and courageous."

While there will be items about sexual politics and related issues, he distanced Gear from Details, which has a strong accent in this "service feature" area. Details is owned by closely held Conde Nast Publications. Nor will it be as music-oriented as Rolling Stone, which is owned by publisher Jann Wenner, or Spin.

Gear's covers will capture people "who are beginning to take off in their careers," he said. This will place Gear in between Details and Wenner's US magazine, whose cover choices are more conservative, and Spin, which favors more cutting-edge subjects.
Guccione will serve as editor in chief of the New York-based magazine and will hire a few English journalists to help him establish it. He identified one as former Sunday Express editor Sue Douglas.
A media analyst said Guccione has his work cut out for him, because Gear's niche is "grossly over-served" with a flood of new entries in recent months such as Swing and POV.

"I think anybody targeting some little sub-niche of the men's market is in for a tough row," said John Masterton, media group editor at Media Industry Newsletter, a weekly newsletter published in New York.
But Masterton said Guccione has "a good sense of smell," and he would benefit from his track record with Spin and his access to capital. He also praised Guccione's aversion to service features.
"How much do guys want to read about sex or how to comb their hair? My belief is that the answer is not that much. So he might be going in the right direction."
